AI Video Discovery: volunteer rating, consent
DRAFT FOR PROJECT-OWNER APPROVAL. Not yet approved; do not send packets with this text until it is.

Purpose
AI Video Discovery is an open-source research project that tries to assess videos and podcasts by what they contain (depth, accuracy, clarity, structure and similar aspects) rather than by how popular they are. Automated assessments can only be trusted if they are compared with careful, independent human judgement. Your ratings are that human judgement.

What you are asked to do
You will read transcripts of public technical podcast episodes published by Changelog Media under the Creative Commons BY-SA 4.0 licence, and rate each episode on ten aspects of content quality using the written descriptions in this file. You can always answer that the transcript does not show something instead of guessing. You may also be asked how relevant each episode is to a few search topics, and, separately and optionally, how much you enjoyed it.
Your first file may instead be a short usability trial: the opening part of one episode, clearly marked as an excerpt. It tests whether these instructions and choices are clear and how long rating takes. Answers in a usability trial are used only to improve the instructions; they are never treated as a rating of the episode.

Time
Each episode takes roughly 50 to 85 minutes to read and rate; a usability trial about 15 to 20 minutes. These are estimates, not measurements. You choose how many episodes to do, and when.

What is recorded
- your ratings, the transcript passages you cite, your notes and any relevance or enjoyment answers;
- the pseudonym the coordinator assigned to you;
- how long each episode was open in your browser, as reported by this file.
This file sends nothing anywhere; you send the ratings file yourself. Your name, e-mail address, IP address and device details are not part of the ratings file.

Pseudonymous, not anonymous
The coordinator knows which person uses which pseudonym, because they sent you this file. They keep that information privately, separate from the ratings, and do not publish it or put it in the project's repository.

Your individual ratings stay private
- Your individual ratings, citations and notes are not published. Only the coordinator, and anyone helping them analyse the results under the same terms, sees them.
- What may be published are aggregate results computed from several raters, for example how far raters agree with each other, or whether automated assessments agree with people. Aggregates are only published when at least three raters contributed to them.
- Notes from a usability trial may be quoted, without your pseudonym, when the instructions are revised. If you do not want a note quoted, write "do not quote" in it.
- Automated assessments of these episodes are hidden from you on purpose. Please do not look for them before you have finished.

Publishing individual ratings needs your separate agreement
Agreeing to this text does not allow anyone to publish your individual ratings. If the project later wants to publish individual ratings as open benchmark data, the coordinator will ask you separately, in writing, and will say exactly what would be published, under what licence and under what name. Only if you say yes in writing are your ratings published, and saying no changes nothing else about your participation.

Re-identification risk
Even without your name, individual records can sometimes be linked back to a person: through the wording of free-text notes, through when files were sent, or because only a few people took part. This is one reason individual records are kept private by default. Please do not put your name, contact details or other personal information in your notes.

How long data is kept
- The coordinator keeps ratings files on their own computer, not on any shared service, for this research.
- Ratings files, and the list that links pseudonyms to people, are deleted at the latest 12 months after your last submission, or sooner if the research ends. Twelve months is enough to finish the analysis, publish the aggregate results and answer questions about them; keeping individual records longer would mostly add risk to you. After deletion, published results can no longer be re-checked against the original ratings, so the project publishes its aggregate statistics together with the code that computed them. Aggregate results that were already published are not deleted.
- If you agreed separately to publication, what was published follows the terms you agreed to then.

Taking part is voluntary
You can stop at any time without giving a reason, and send partial work or nothing at all.

Withdrawing
You can ask the coordinator to withdraw your ratings at any time. Your ratings file and your entry in the pseudonym list are then deleted, and your ratings are excluded from every later analysis. One limit applies: aggregate results that were already published cannot be recalculated retroactively.

Questions and contact
Contact the coordinator through the same channel through which you received this file. Please do not post your ratings file, or this file, publicly (for example in a GitHub issue): they contain a code that identifies your packet.

There is no payment, and there are no known risks beyond the time you spend and the re-identification risk described above. The project cannot give legal guarantees about how third parties use published aggregate results.

By ticking the box below you confirm that you are at least 18 years old, that you have read this text, and that you agree to take part on these terms.
